orders.explanation: Transcript 1 methodically locates the upstream fix, applies the correct patch in `Catalog.__iter__`, updates tests and CHANGES, and validates it against the full Sphinx test suite and an end-to-end reproduction. Transcript 2 proposes a simpler but incorrect change in `Message.__init__` and lacks comprehensive verification.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it precisely identified and back-ported the upstream Sphinx fix (modifying Catalog.__iter__), added the matching regression test and CHANGES entry, and fully verified all affected tests and an end-to-end build. Transcript 1 applied a more ad hoc change in the wrong place and failed to integrate the official test and CHANGES updates.

Transcript 1 methodically identifies the bug in `signature_from_str`, computes the correct default‐index formula, applies a precise patch, and exhaustively verifies it against edge cases and the Sphinx build, whereas Transcript 2’s attempt is disorganized, introduces errors in handling defaults, and never cleanly completes or validates the fix.

Transcript 1 deeply diagnoses the missing-defaults bug by tracing AST defaults, implements a precise code fix in signature_from_str, and exhaustively validates it with unit tests and an HTML build. Transcript 2 only lists files and greps without proposing or testing a solution.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a deep root-cause analysis—examining the patched libstdc++ code, tracing heap and facet registration order, reproducing the crash, crafting a minimal fix in `user_init()` to force early facet registration, and fully verifying with multiple builds, GDB and Valgrind. Transcript 2 flails with incorrect overrides, wrapping attempts, and only superficially tests a locale workaround without understanding or proof.

Transcript 2 correctly diagnoses the root cause (lazy facet allocation using the custom heap) and implements a precise fix by calling std::_Facet_Register_impl() in user_init(), ensuring allocations happen before the custom heap is active. Transcript 1 merely circumvents the issue by forcing the C locale on std::cout, a narrower workaround, after many failed attempts. Transcript 2’s solution is more robust and directly addresses the underlying bug.

Transcript 1 methodically tracks a plan, catches and fixes a proto numbering mistake, generates and verifies the server with end-to-end tests, and uses the correct int32 types and default behavior. Transcript 2 contains proto and code-signature errors, inconsistent types, and less thorough validation. Hence Transcript 1 is from the more capable model.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it not only implements all required components correctly on the first try (only needing to fix a proto field number), but also maintains and updates an explicit execution plan, uses comprehensive end-to-end verification scripts (including port reachability checks), and demonstrates a higher level of structure and reliability. Transcript 1, by contrast, contains a couple of coding missteps that require correction and lacks the same degree of planning and post-deployment validation.

Transcript 2 quickly arrives at a minimal, correct solution—switching to scipy.linalg.eig—validates it against all tests, and demonstrates a measurable speedup over the numpy reference. Transcript 1 invests in a custom Numba Hessenberg/QR routine but never achieves a working, faster implementation.

Transcript 1 shows a deep, systematic exploration—benchmarking multiple algorithms, diagnosing subtle numerical bugs, and finally implementing a full Numba‐accelerated QR‐based solver with Wilkinson shifts and deflation. Its thorough testing and iterative refinement indicate a far more capable model than the trivial numpy or scipy‐based solutions.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a coherent plan, robust environment setup, precise Git operations, conflict resolution with a fully correct implementation, and exhaustive automated and randomized testing to verify generalization. Transcript 2 is far more ad hoc, struggles with environment configuration, performs only minimal example checks, and lacks stress-testing or detailed conflict resolution.

Transcript 2 demonstrates a clearer, more systematic approach: it sets out an explicit plan, inspects base, branch, and merge with precision, writes a self-documenting implementation with a detailed docstring, and then performs extensive randomized and edge‐case testing to validate generalization. Transcript 1 is more ad‐hoc, less organized, and stops short of the robust verification seen in Transcript 2.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more thorough, systematic approach—complete planning, error handling, subjectAltName inclusion, robust Python parsing and timezone handling, extensive verification steps and key–cert matching—whereas Transcript 2 is simpler and omits several best practices.

Transcript 2 shows a more systematic and robust approach: it begins with an explicit planning step, verifies the environment, includes a Subject Alternative Name extension, rigorously checks file permissions, matches key and certificate moduli, handles Python SSL decoding edge cases, and iteratively debugs and refines the script. Transcript 1, while correct, is more straightforward and less thorough.

Transcript 1 demonstrates a far more systematic, robust approach: it detects the lack of a compiler, installs the correct toolchain, extracts and configures with full gcov flags, builds, installs, and then rigorously verifies coverage symbols, `.gcda` outputs, and `gcov` functionality. Transcript 2 is more ad hoc, fails to fully verify instrumentation, and even uses `libsqlite3-dev` unnecessarily.

Transcript 2 is from the more capable model because it demonstrates richer environment discovery, a structured planning API, precise use of coverage flags, full end-to-end verification of gcov symbols and .gcda file generation, and cleanup—all in a clear, methodical workflow. Transcript 1, while correct, is less thorough in verifying actual coverage instrumentation and lacks the planning structure.
